tip_title: August Is Prime Time for Deer Strikes and Storm Damage. Here's the Coverage That Pays for That.
topic: Comprehensive Auto Coverage - Summer Animal Strike and Storm Damage
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: August Is Prime Time for Deer Strikes and Storm Damage. Here's the Coverage That Pays for That.**

Collision coverage pays when you hit another car or a fixed object. Comprehensive is the one that handles everything else — a deer that walks into your path, a tree branch that falls on your hood during a thunderstorm, hail damage, a cracked windshield from road debris. Georgia summers bring all of that, and August is no exception. The thing a lot of people don't realize is that comprehensive and collision are separate coverages, and some drivers drop one without fully understanding which scenarios they're walking away from. If you're not sure which ones you're carrying right now, your declarations page will tell you.

Want to make sure you've got the right coverage before storm season wraps up? Your Peachy agent can take a look with you.

📖 [Learn more from The Zebra](https://www.thezebra.com/auto-insurance/insurance-guide/comprehensive-vs-collision/)
summary: Covers comprehensive auto coverage (non-collision events like animal strikes, storm damage, hail, and falling objects) as a distinct coverage from collision, framed around August storm season and deer activity rather than the prior tip's general collision-vs-comprehensive explanation.
scoring_notes: Prior tip on this subject (June 29) covered the general functional difference between collision and comprehensive. This tip approaches it from a seasonal/scenario angle — specifically August storm damage and animal strikes — so it qualifies as a different angle. Repeat subject noted in scoring_notes per dedup rules. Source (thezebra.com) is not on the primary trusted list, but the content is solid and corroborated by investopedia.com (also not on primary list). Both audiences have meaningful auto exposure and the seasonal hook is strong. Timeliness is high because Georgia thunderstorm activity peaks mid-summer and deer activity picks up in late summer heading into fall.

tip_title: Your Kid Is Heading to College. Does Your Home Policy Know That?
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Kid Is Heading to College. Does Your Home Policy Know That?**

If you've got a college-bound kid moving into a dorm this fall, there's a decent chance their stuff is already covered under your homeowners policy — typically up to 10% of your personal property limit while they're living on campus. The catch is that 10% can disappear fast when you start adding up a laptop, a TV, AirPods, and a few hundred dollars in clothes. And once they move off campus into an apartment, most of that coverage goes away entirely, which is when a renters policy starts making a lot of sense. Before they leave for school, it's worth pulling up your declarations page and seeing what you're actually working with.

Not sure how your policy handles it? Your Peachy agent can walk through your coverage with you before the semester starts.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/college-students-and-renters-insurance)
summary: Covers how homeowners insurance extends to college students living in dorms (personal property sub-limit) and why that coverage typically ends when a student moves off campus into an apartment, framed as a back-to-school action item.
scoring_notes: August is peak back-to-school/move-in month. East Cobb audience skews toward established families with teens and college-age kids — this hits exactly that demographic. Homeownership rate of 78% means most readers have a homeowners policy this applies to. Not a repeat subject from the last 6 months. Actionable in the next 30 days before semester starts. Source is III (trusted). Note: III's college/renters page is the best available trusted-source anchor for this angle — candidate list didn't include this exact topic but the III domain is on the trusted list and this tip is solidly supported by published III content on this subject.

tip_title: Before the Storm Hits, Your Yard Might Be Your Biggest Insurance Problem
topic: Hurricane Preparedness - Property Protection Before a Storm
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Before the Storm Hits, Your Yard Might Be Your Biggest Insurance Problem**

We're in peak Atlantic hurricane season right now, and here's something most homeowners don't think about until it's too late: anything unsecured in your yard becomes a projectile in hurricane-force winds. That patio furniture, that loose tree branch hanging over your roof, the decorative stuff sitting along your fence line — all of it. Standard homeowners policies cover sudden wind damage, but a claim gets complicated fast when the damage could have been prevented with basic prep. FEMA recommends trimming or removing trees that could fall onto your house and clearing yard debris before a storm is ever named.

Take thirty minutes this weekend to walk your yard with fresh eyes. It's the kind of thing that can make a real difference in whether you're filing a claim or just cleaning up.

Not sure how your policy handles wind damage or what your hurricane deductible looks like? Your Peachy agent can pull up your declarations page and walk through it with you.

📖 [Learn more from FEMA](https://www.fema.gov/blog/six-ways-prepare-your-home-hurricane)
summary: Covers pre-storm property preparation as an insurance risk-reduction step, specifically securing yard items and trimming trees that could cause wind damage — framed as a mid-peak-season action item distinct from prior tips on hurricane deductibles and declaration page checks.
scoring_notes: August is statistically peak Atlantic hurricane season. Both East Cobb audiences are high-homeowner (78%), so this lands well for both. Prior hurricane tips covered the declaration page review (June 22), the wind/hurricane percentage-deductible mechanic (July 24), and a NFIP vs. private flood comparison (July 20). This tip takes a completely different angle — physical property prep as a claims-prevention and coverage-context action item — so no meaningful overlap. High actionability because the reader can literally go outside this weekend.
